A.explanation: Gives only $25 \text{ N}$ vertical component, so its anticlockwise moment about O is only half the $200 \text{ N m}$ needed to balance the weight.

B.explanation: Results from using the wrong trigonometric component of tension, such as $T \cos 30^{\circ}$ for the vertical lift, when resolving perpendicular to the $4.0 \text{ m}$ beam.

C.explanation: Is about $100 \cos 30^{\circ}$, which incorrectly resolves the $100 \text{ N}$ weight instead of resolving the tension into $T \sin 30^{\circ}$.

D.explanation: Gives vertical component $100 \sin 30^{\circ} = 50 \text{ N}$ at $4.0 \text{ m}$, whose $200 \text{ N m}$ moment exactly balances the weight moment.

hints: Notice the $100 \text{ N}$ weight of the uniform $4.0 \text{ m}$ beam acts at its centre, $2.0 \text{ m}$ from hinge O.
Take moments about O so the unknown hinge force has zero moment, leaving only the weight and the cord tension.
Resolve the tension into a vertical component using the $30^{\circ}$ angle at X, then equate its $4.0 \text{ m}$ anticlockwise moment to the clockwise weight moment.
walkthrough: Identify the pivot for moments as hinge O. The hinge force then has zero perpendicular distance and does not appear in the moment equation.

The uniform beam weight $W = 100 \text{ N}$ acts downwards at the midpoint, so its perpendicular distance from O is $2.0 \text{ m}$. Clockwise moment is $W \times 2.0 = 100 \times 2.0 = 200 \text{ N m}$.
The cord pulls at X at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Only the vertical component lifts the beam, $T_v = T \sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5T$.
Its perpendicular distance from O is the full beam length $4.0 \text{ m}$, so anticlockwise moment is $T_v \times 4.0 = 0.5T \times 4.0 = 2.0T$.
For equilibrium, sum of moments about O is zero: $2.0T = 200$. Hence $T = 100 \text{ N}$ with unit check $\text{N m} / \text{m} = \text{N}$. This is option D.
